name: Victor Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday sound like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead a town brass band, play cornet at ceremonies, record rehearsal parts and teach three young players. I have a music master’s and have spent decades keeping forty musicians together through a long march. I like the small nod from the back row when the tempo finally holds, though I dislike chasing a fee after the chairs are folded.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that pay sit with life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a school office, our children are grown, and the mortgage still has years on it. The band and ceremony fees are typical for this work; we have four months of expenses saved and a few other bands nearby. I keep paper scores and a wall calendar and have never used AI to run the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the committee that a faster booking form is fine if the paid rehearsal date and conductor fee still sit in ink. I would keep the score on the stand and lead the band myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school-office wage and our band season cover the mortgage, and four months saved would carry a brief gap. I still want a written fee because the committee has paid late after a parade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid band and pupil calls and request written conductor, rehearsal and cancellation fees before the winter parade. In the plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate and compare the figure with our mortgage before setting a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the current season. A brass band can miss a turn, but our paid dates are on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on ink if the form is faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parade fee came six weeks late once. A written amount and payment date let me plan the next mortgage debit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the estimate end bandleading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I do not know what it says yet. My partner and I would put the real number beside bills before deciding anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the committee that a generated rehearsal track may show notes, but it cannot watch a tired cornet section breathe. I would ask which recorded parts and preparation hours still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rehearsal recordings are a modest but regular fee, roughly one in ten of my music income. I think the committee will buy fewer, and even that cut belongs in our household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for written band and recording rates and keep my paid pupil lessons. If the two monthly rehearsal-track orders stop during disruption, I would postpone the planned amplifier upgrade until a signed paid ceremony covers it; I would not pay for a tool I have never used just to make a track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a regular part of my own pay. A shiny amplifier cannot fill the gap left by two unpaid recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a learner who asks about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say to listen to the note with the teacher and practise slowly. I have never used AI for the band, and I am not beginning with a pupil’s recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the committee offer a free upgrade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it supplies equipment without taking my fee, I would consider it later. Today the signed ceremony must cover any upgrade I buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI in 2028 could make rehearsal parts before robot players can carry brass around 2031. I would ask for signed live parade and concert calls now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the rehearsal-track fees to end in 2028 and the committee may pay less preparation. The live band is still booked, so I would not call the whole chair lost today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total track and preparation invoices and secure signed parade and concert dates. In the first year after 2028, if recording fees end and paid live calls also fall, I would apply for a posted paid community-band conductor job only if it accepts my music master’s and years leading brass, pays for in-person rehearsal and correction, and gives written net pay after travel replacing the losses with a bus home; I would keep current paid band and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected track loss and possible preparation cut, but four months saved gives us time to compare real jobs. I would worry much more if the live dates fell as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a new band pay a conductor in an AGI world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person has to hear when the back row drifts and bring forty players back together. I would read the actual posting to see if those live hours are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would robots carry brass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card places capable hands-on players around 2031. A track order can stop in 2028 before any such player arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the committee that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to price the work of training a young section leader. Robot players around 2034 are a later question than paying today’s rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tracks may earn less before 2031, but I can still teach a player to give a clear entry. I would rather keep a paid apprenticeship inside the band than buy a new course for myself on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask the committee for a written two-year band renewal with paid rehearsal, preparation and a weekly hour mentoring a young brass leader. In the first year after 2031 I would keep the band and three pupils if those hours are signed and paid; if track fees and live calls both fall, I would seek a posted paid school-band director vacancy only if my master’s and band-leading years qualify, live human rehearsal and correction are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus fits, keeping current paid work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious that track fees could fall over five years, even if the present band has dates. A trainee learns by standing beside a paid leader, not by reading a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the trainee for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask for one paid mentoring hour each week beside rehearsal. A committee promise is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a school posted such a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No particular school has offered me a post. I would look only at an actual paid vacancy that accepts my record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger players that a decade until AGI by 2036 is time to put rehearsal and mentoring fees into the band contract. Robot brass players around 2039 do not sign a parade call today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer long marches, but I have no pension figure and no date set. The band and pupils pay today, with four months saved if one season runs short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and written band renewal, then save five percent of any extra cleared ceremony fee after mortgage, food and fuel toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid band and pupil hours while they are booked, and if track and live fees both fall seek a posted paid community-band conductor role only if my master’s and brass leadership qualify, paid live rehearsal remains, written net pay after travel replaces the losses and the bus runs; I would not leave current paid work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording work, while the present band and four-month reserve support the bills. A pension estimate will be useful, but it is not a paid concert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no extra ceremony fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing new goes into savings that month. Six months is a target, not what we already hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire as soon as the estimate arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would put the actual figure beside bills and health. I have no retirement date agreed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because track fees could stop before I find another paid band if live calls fall too. Signed parade dates, an actual conductor vacancy accepting my master’s and a written net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the committee pays a young leader to learn the cue. Forty brass players do not find one tempo because a computer prints a number.

headlineQuote: Forty brass players do not find one tempo because a computer prints a number.
portrait: Victor is a **senior brass leader** with a music master’s, forty band players, ceremonies and three pupils.
His **typical pay**, four-month reserve, mortgage and some nearby bands support present work.
He uses a **paper score** and has never used AI for the band.
He seeks **paid mentoring** inside the current band and considers a posted human conductor role only after dual fee losses.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could end recorded-track fees before any replacement band work is available.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed parade dates**, a posted conductor vacancy accepting his master’s and written replacement net after travel.
